results.claim: The literal simultaneous pyramid problem is an interval-permutation problem. Put m=ell+1 and a_i=min(r+i-1,n). If pos(i) is one plus the final row size occupied by colour i, then solutions are exactly permutations satisfying a_i-m+1 <= pos(i) <= a_i+1, clipped to [1,n]. Thus the answer is the permanent of this interval matrix.
results.proof_sketch: The final multiplicities, including zero for the omitted colour, are exactly 0,1,...,n-1. Assigning them to the n labelled colours is therefore equivalent to a permutation pos of [n]. Colour i loses e_i=a_i-(pos(i)-1) objects. The physical condition 0<=e_i<=m is precisely a_i-m+1<=pos(i)<=a_i+1, with positions restricted to [1,n]. Conversely, every admissible permutation defines a unique nonnegative removal vector satisfying the cap, so the correspondence is bijective and the indicated permanent counts it.

results.claim: Let A_{n,ell,r} denote the answer, with 0<=r<=n and m=ell+1. Then A_{n,ell,0}=1; if r>=1 and m<r, then A_{n,ell,r}=0; and if r>=1, m>=r, and n<m, then A_{n,ell,r}=r!(r+1)^(n-r). For n>=m there is an explicit finite-state formula given below.
results.proof_sketch: For r=0, the initial and target multiplicity multisets are both 0,1,...,n-1. Their equal total sizes force the sum of the nonnegative removals to be zero, hence every removal is zero. If m<r, whichever colour receives final multiplicity zero must lose at least r>m objects. If n<m, every initial multiplicity is at most n<m, so the cap is inactive; the source's flatorial enumeration is r!(r+1)^(n-r). These cases and the active case below partition all admissible parameters.

results.claim: Assume 1<=r<=m<=n and set q=m-r. Let U={1-r,...,q}, let S be the q-subsets of U, and I={1,...,q}. Define T_{S,S'} as the number of x in S union {q+1} such that S'={y-1: y in (S union {q+1}) minus {x}} is a q-subset of U. For S={s_1<...<s_q}, put w(S)=r! product_{j=1}^q(s_j+r-j+1). Then A_{n,ell,r}=e_I^T T^(n-m) w.
results.proof_sketch: The ordinary colours i<=n-r have permitted positions i-q through i+r; the last r colours have lower bound n-m+1. Put K=n-m. Thus only ordinary colours occur in the first K positions. After k positions, record each introduced but unused ordinary colour i by its offset i-k. The q offsets form a state S, initially I. The next eligible colour has offset q+1. Choosing the next colour and decrementing all remaining offsets gives exactly T; rejecting offsets below 1-r enforces every right deadline. After K steps, lower bounds are automatic. An ordinary colour with terminal offset s has deadline s+r among the last m positions. For s_1<...<s_q, placing these colours in deadline order gives product_j(s_j+r-j+1) injections. The r terminal colours fill the remaining positions in r! orders. This proves the formula, including q=0.

results.claim: For fixed ell and r with 1<=r<=m=ell+1, the complete ordinary generating function is rational: G_{ell,r}(z)=sum_{n>=r}A_{n,ell,r}z^n = r! sum_{n=r}^{m-1}(r+1)^(n-r)z^n + z^m e_I^T(I-zT)^(-1)w. Consequently A_{n,ell,r} satisfies an explicit constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most binomial(m,r) for n>=m.
results.proof_sketch: The finite sum is exactly the inactive-cap range r<=n<m. Formally expanding (I-zT)^(-1)=sum_{k>=0}z^kT^k makes the coefficient of z^(m+k) equal e_I^T T^k w, the active formula. Hence the displayed generating function contains every coefficient and is rational. The state space has D=binomial(m,q)=binomial(m,r) elements. If the characteristic polynomial is x^D+c_1x^(D-1)+...+c_D, Cayley-Hamilton gives A_{n+D}+c_1A_{n+D-1}+...+c_DA_n=0 for every n>=m.

results.claim: The physical simultaneous problem is generally not the naive intersection of the displacement bounds 'ell left' and 'r right.' For example, n=4, ell=1, r=2 has exactly two physical solutions, represented by 1234 and 1243, whereas the naive two-sided displacement class has seven permutations.
results.proof_sketch: Here m=2 and the initial multiplicities are (2,3,4,4). The physical intervals are pos(1) in [1,3], pos(2) in [2,4], and pos(3),pos(4) in [3,4]. Bijectivity forces pos(1)=1 and pos(2)=2, leaving the two stated words. Exact enumeration under the naive bounds i-1<=pos(i)<=i+2 instead gives 1234, 1243, 1324, 1342, 2134, 2143, and 2314.

final_writeup:
Set m=ell+1 and let A_{n,ell,r} count solutions obtained by applying the Section 3 per-colour removal cap to the relaxed initial pyramid of Section 7, where 0<=r<=n.

Colour i initially has a_i=min(r+i-1,n) objects. The target pyramid has multiplicities 1,...,n-1, together with multiplicity zero for the omitted colour. Write pos(i)=k when colour i receives final multiplicity k-1. The pos(i) form a permutation of [n], and colour i loses

e_i=a_i-pos(i)+1.

Consequently the exact admissibility condition is

a_i-m+1 <= pos(i) <= a_i+1,

clipped to [1,n]. Therefore

A_{n,ell,r}=per(1{max(1,a_i-m+1)<=k<=min(n,a_i+1)})_{i,k=1}^n.

This permanent already gives an exact enumeration. The following transfer construction gives a finite-state formula, rational generating function, and recurrence.

First dispose of the boundary regimes. If r=0, the initial and target multiplicity multisets are both 0,1,...,n-1; equality of their totals forces every nonnegative removal to be zero, so A_{n,ell,0}=1. If r>=1 and m<r, some colour must be reduced to zero although every initial multiplicity is at least r>m, so A_{n,ell,r}=0. If r>=1, m>=r, and n<m, the cap is inactive because every initial multiplicity is at most n<m. The flatorial result from Section 7 then gives

A_{n,ell,r}=r!(r+1)^(n-r).

It remains to consider 1<=r<=m<=n. Put q=m-r and U={1-r,...,q}. Let the states be the q-subsets S of U, and let I={1,...,q}. Define

T_{S,S'}=#{x in S union {q+1}: S'={y-1: y in (S union {q+1}) minus {x}} is a q-subset of U}.

For S={s_1<...<s_q}, define

w(S)=r! product_{j=1}^q(s_j+r-j+1).

Then

A_{n,ell,r}=e_I^T T^(n-m)w.

Indeed, the ordinary colours i<=n-r have initial sizes r+i-1 and permitted positions i-q,...,i+r. The final r colours have initial size n and can occur only in positions n-m+1,...,n. Set K=n-m. During the first K positions only ordinary colours can occur. After k positions, exactly q introduced ordinary colours remain unused. Recording their labels relative to k produces a q-subset S of U, initially I. The next eligible colour has relative label q+1. Choosing the next colour and decrementing every remaining label is exactly one transition of T. Excluding a successor below 1-r enforces the upper-position deadlines, while the introduction schedule enforces the lower bounds.

After K transitions, the last m positions remain. An ordinary colour with offset s has relative deadline s+r, and its lower bound is now automatic. If the remaining offsets are s_1<...<s_q, place these colours in increasing deadline order. At step j there are s_j+r-(j-1) available positions, producing the stated product. The r equal-sized terminal colours can be assigned to the remaining slots in r! ways. Empty states and products give the same proof when q=0.

For fixed ell and r with 1<=r<=m, the complete ordinary generating function is therefore

G_{ell,r}(z)=sum_{n>=r}A_{n,ell,r}z^n
=r! sum_{n=r}^{m-1}(r+1)^(n-r)z^n+z^m e_I^T(I-zT)^(-1)w.

It is rational. Since T has D=binomial(m,r) states, its characteristic polynomial supplies a homogeneous constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most D for every base index n>=m. The r=0 and m<r regimes are respectively constant-one and zero sequences and have trivial recurrences.

This is the literal simultaneous physical model, not the naive intersection of the separate displacement descriptions. For n=4, ell=1, r=2, the physical class has only 1234 and 1243, while the naive two-sided displacement class has seven permutations. Thus the formulas cover every admissible parameter regime and fully resolve the requested enumeration.
